_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 9 Data Problems. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. REORDERING REVIEWED 2026-09-24: the film plays 'named' third (right after twokinds), where LESSON['lecture'] has it fifth, appended after 'choose' (lesson-9.py lines 187-196 give the first four parts, 243-249 append the fifth). Kept deliberately, not by default: twokinds and named teach the SAME distinction twice in different words (discrete/categorical, then named/numerical) over the SAME eight-children pet data, so grouping them lets the reinforcement land while the examples are still on screen; moving 'named' to the lesson's own position would break the views-then-choose pair with an unrelated return to vocabulary immediately before the recap. Every figure spoken is the lesson's own data - the pets count 2,3,2,1 and the favourite pet 4,2,1,1, both of eight children - and the film's table, bar chart and pictogram are all drawn from one array each, so the words, the tally, the bars and the axis cannot disagree. The only wrong cases shown are marked as wrong: a story is not a data problem, one and a half pets does not exist, and a cat cannot be added to a dog. OBJECTIVES REVIEWED 2026-09-24: 'named' carries no codes - it is pure classification (name cards vs a numerical panel, no device drawn) and does not teach 3MD.03 ('using computing devices'); twokinds already earns 3MD.03 properly, drawing ART.figure('tablet') running the lesson's own form.
title: Data Problems
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Identify problems that can be solved through the collection and interpretation of data.
Know how to record discrete and categorical data, using computing devices.
Identify and investigate different ways of representing discrete and categorical data, using a digital tool.

beats.say: Which snack should the tuck shop sell? Ask every child, and count.
Some problems are solved by collecting data and reading what it says.
Three school problems. Which snack should the tuck shop sell?
How many chairs for the concert? Count the parents who are coming.
When is the playground busiest? Count the children at each break.
Collecting data means asking or counting. Interpreting it means reading what the numbers say.
Not every problem is a data problem. What your story is about is not a count.
Eight children answered two questions on a tablet. How many pets do you have?

at.howmany: How many pets do you have?

beats.say: Discrete data is whole numbers you count. Zero pets, one pet, two pets.
Never one and a half. You cannot have half a cat.
The second question: which pet would you most like? Cat, dog, fish or rabbit.

at.like: which pet would you most like

beats.say: Those are categories, not counts. That is categorical data.
The form on the tablet counted each answer as it came in.
Some data is a name. Red, blue, dog, cat, came by bus.
You cannot add a cat to a dog. You can only count how many of each.

at.cannot: cannot add a cat to a dog

beats.say: Other data is numerical. It is a number you counted or measured.

at.number: a number you counted or measured

beats.say: How many pets, how tall, how many minutes. Numbers can be added and put in order.
Here is the pet data, and a digital tool can show it three ways.
A table gives the exact numbers. Two children have no pets, three have one.
A bar chart shows the biggest at a glance. One pet has the tallest bar.
A pictogram draws one picture for each answer. You count the pictures.
Categories work too. Four children chose a cat, and two chose a dog.
The three views never disagree. They are the same eight answers.
Each view is best for a different question.
Exactly how many children have two pets? The table says two.
Which pet is the class favourite? The bar chart shows it at a glance: cat.

at.which: Which pet is the class favourite

beats.say: Count them by eye? The pictogram. Interpreting is reading the right view.

at.interpret: Interpreting is reading the right view

beats.say: Collect the data, then read what it says. That is a problem solved with data.
Counts are discrete data. Categories are categorical data.
A table gives the exact numbers. A bar chart shows the biggest at a glance.
A pictogram gives one picture for each one, so you can count them by eye.
